title: Bringing back stupid
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman responds to a Labour Party conference speech by England's education minister Lucy Powell, who defended reforms that would partly undo the Gove-era changes. He argues that good intentions are plentiful in education while good ideas are scarce, because feedback is slow and causes are hard to trace. His main evidence is the UK's natural experiment: Scotland and Wales followed expert advice with skills-centred curricula and declined, while England bucked the trend. He also shows that Powell's claims about absence and young people not in education, employment or training are not borne out by the Scottish and Welsh comparison. The core of his critique is the plan for new vocational GCSEs, which he expects to become watered-down classroom subjects that schools will use to channel advantaged students toward easier grades, as happened under the previous Labour government. He concludes that Powell means well but should turn back before dismantling reforms that worked.
points: The shortage in education is of good ideas rather than good intentions, because slow and ambiguous feedback lets people stay convinced of what they wish were true.
Scotland and Wales adopted expert-endorsed curricula built on transferable skills and declined in PISA mathematics, while England, which kept a knowledge-focused path, did not.
Attendance and NEET figures do not support the charge that academic reforms caused harm, since the other UK nations show little difference or worse persistent absence.
Genuine vocational qualifications are demanding and need real equipment and expertise, so schools will most likely deliver pen-and-paper imitations that Ashman labels crapademic subjects.
Incentives matter: if the new courses offer easier grades, schools will steer more advantaged students into them, repeating the 2000s equivalence problem.
quotes: There is no shortage of good intentions in education; the shortage is of good ideas. In education, feedback is slow in coming and often, effects cannot easily be traced back to their causes.
So did Wales with its own curriculum reforms. Both centred on non-existent transferrable skills and were vague about knowledge.

Following quite different policies to England, endorsed by education experts, has led to little difference in the number of young people not in education, employment or training, with persistent absence from school being considerably higher in Scotland than in England.
Rather than true vocational qualifications, these have all the hallmarks of turning into ‘crapademic’ subjects, taught in regular classrooms, with students working with pen and paper, or on a laptop.

But genuine, industry-aligned vocational qualifications are rigorous and challenging and the chances are that students struggling with basic English and mathematics are unlikely to do well. So, they will be offered crapademic qualifications instead, feeding the snobbery Powell wishes to end.

The further risk is that schools will become incentivised to channel more advantaged students into these courses in the hope of easier grades. That’s exactly what happened under the Blair-Brown government of the 2000s.
The problem is that good intentions are not enough and, in education, are often responsible for excesses and horrors that let down the same disadvantaged young people they seek to help.
